analysis.one_liner: Requires testing every cattle carcass for mad cow disease before it enters the food supply.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Agriculture Committee and died without a vote when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended federal meat inspection law to require a test for bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease) on every cattle carcass and part intended for human food [S2] [S3]. Only government inspectors would conduct the tests, and meat slaughtering and packing plants would pay fees covering the cost [S2] [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of beef and beef products, who would get a government test for mad cow disease on every carcass entering the food supply, at a time when the first U.S. mad cow case had just been found and other countries were restricting American beef [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires post-mortem testing of all cattle carcasses and parts intended for human consumption for bovine spongiform encephalopathy [S2] [S3].
Testing must be conducted only by Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service personnel, keeping the testing in government hands rather than company self-reporting [S2] [S3].

Allows the Agriculture Secretary to delay testing for cattle under a certain age only if no accurate test exists for that age, with yearly evaluations and reports to Congress during any delay [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Slaughtering, meat-canning, salting, packing, rendering, and other meat establishments, which would pay fees covering all testing costs, likely passing some of that cost on in beef prices [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Meat establishments bear the full cost of testing through fees, and those costs would likely be passed at least partly to consumers through higher beef prices [S2] [S3].

The bill itself acknowledges a practical limit: if no accurate test exists for cattle under a certain age, the testing requirement for those animals can be delayed until one is available, so universal coverage would depend on test availability [S2] [S3].

Testing every carcass goes far beyond the sampling-based surveillance the U.S. already used; critics argued the disease's long incubation and low prevalence made universal testing of young cattle a costly safeguard of uncertain benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a straightforward food-safety guarantee — every carcass tested by government inspectors, with industry covering the cost — during a period of real public concern about mad cow disease. The honest counterweight is cost: universal testing of tens of millions of cattle annually is expensive, and the bill's own age-based delay provision shows the science of detecting the disease in young animals was not settled. A well-designed version would still have given consumers far more assurance than the status quo.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, got no further action, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller introduced the Mad Cow Testing Act of 2004 on January 20, 2004, one month after the first U.S. case of mad cow disease was announced in December 2003.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day and no further action was ever taken on it [S1] [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat slaughtering and packing companies were better off, since they avoided the testing fees and operational burden the bill would have imposed; consumers did not get the carcass-by-carcass testing it promised.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only named sponsor.

for.name: One House Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 20, 2004 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with the committee taking no action, no path to a vote existed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Democratic sponsors and never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists of who supported or opposed it.

industries.note: The bill would have required these plants to pay fees covering government testing of every carcass for mad cow disease. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against consumers' interest in tested beef; by the bill's death, packers avoided the cost and consumers kept the status quo.

Universal testing would have added costs upstream but could have restored export markets that closed after the December 2003 mad cow discovery, since trading partners like Japan demanded testing. The bill died, so ranchers faced neither the costs nor those market benefits from it.
The bill would have expanded APHIS's role by making its personnel the sole testers of all cattle carcasses, with fee collections funding the work.
